title: Inversion after negative and limiting adverbials
tagline: Move the adverbial to the front, swap subject and auxiliary — and the sentence gains weight.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (NO SOONER, ONLY, UNDER, LITTLE)
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (did / had / than / when)
Writing Part 1 — essay: emphatic, formal sentences
Speaking Parts 3 and 4 — sounding emphatic when you argue
why: Inversion is one of the clearest markers of C1 writing: the same idea, said with more force and in a more formal register. C1 Advanced tests it directly in Part 4, where the key word is often the adverbial itself, and rewards it in the essay. The rule is mechanical; what takes practice is knowing which expressions trigger it and where the inversion happens.

diagrams.title: From neutral to emphatic

before.text: I have never seen such a mess in my life.

after.text: Never in my life have I seen such a mess.

steps: Take the negative or limiting adverbial (never in my life) to the front.
Invert the auxiliary and the subject, as in a question: have I.
If there is no auxiliary, add do / does / did: Little did she know…

rows.label: Pattern
cells: ADVERBIAL + [subordinate clause, normal order] + aux + subject + verb

rows.label: Example
cells: Rarely have I heard such a bad excuse.
Not until the bell rang did he stop talking.

rows.label: Typical triggers
cells: never, rarely, seldom, under no circumstances
not until, only when, only after, only once

rows.label: Common error
cells: Not until did the bell ring…

formula.ex: Never before / Only then / No sooner

head: Trigger
Structure
Example
rows: Never / Rarely / Seldom
+ aux + subject
Seldom does a debut novel sell this well.
No sooner … than
No sooner + had + subject + participle + than …
No sooner had we sat down than the lights went out.
Hardly / Scarcely … when
Hardly + had + subject + participle + when …
Hardly had the match started when it began to pour.
Not until / Only when / Only after
adverbial + clause + aux + subject
Not until I reread it did I notice the mistake.
Not only … but (also)
Not only + aux + subject … but (also) …
Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.
Under no circumstances / On no account
+ modal + subject
Under no circumstances should you share your password.
So + adjective … that / Such + noun … that
So/Such … + be + subject + that …
So loud was the music that the neighbours complained.
Little
Little + did + subject + know / realise
Little did they realise what was coming.

use.point: Emphasising how unusual or extreme something is

examples.text: Never before had the school reached the national final.
examples.note: past perfect: never before that moment

examples.text: Rarely do you meet someone who listens as carefully as Nadia.
Nowhere else will you find a view like this one.

use.point: Showing that two events happened almost at the same time

examples.text: No sooner had Mateo pressed 'send' than he spotted the typo.
examples.note: no sooner … than, always past perfect

examples.text: Hardly had the assembly begun when the fire alarm went off.
Not until the results were published did anyone believe we had won.
examples.note: the inversion comes in the main clause, after the time clause

use.point: Limiting: only in one way, only at one moment

examples.text: Only by practising every day can you master a language.
Only after the interview did I realise how nervous I had been.
Not only does the plan cost less, but it also creates jobs.
examples.note: an essay favourite: two arguments in one sentence

examples.text: Under no circumstances should candidates open the paper before the signal.
On no account must this door be left unlocked.
examples.note: passive after the modal is fine

examples.text: Such was the demand that the tickets sold out in an hour.

watch_out.wrong: Never I have seen such a mess.
watch_out.right: Never have I seen such a mess.
watch_out.why: The auxiliary must come before the subject, as in a question.

watch_out.wrong: Rarely she complains about the workload.
watch_out.right: Rarely does she complain about the workload.
watch_out.why: With no auxiliary in the original, add do / does / did and use the bare infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: Not until did the bell ring he stopped.
watch_out.right: Not until the bell rang did he stop.
watch_out.why: The time clause keeps normal order; the main clause inverts.

watch_out.wrong: No sooner had we arrived when the show started.
watch_out.right: No sooner had we arrived than the show started.
watch_out.why: No sooner pairs with than; hardly / scarcely pair with when.

watch_out.wrong: Only yesterday did I have seen the email.
watch_out.right: Only yesterday did I see the email.
watch_out.why: After did the verb is the bare infinitive — never a participle.

watch_out.wrong: Not only she sings but also she dances.
watch_out.right: Not only does she sing, but she also dances.
watch_out.why: Invert only in the first clause; the second keeps normal order.

dialogue.title: The night the power went out
dialogue.context: Miss Vega asks Liam and Sofia to retell what happened at the school concert, using the emphatic structures they have been studying.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: So, tell the class what happened on Friday — and make it sound dramatic.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: No sooner had the choir started the first song than every light in the hall went out.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Never in my life have I heard four hundred people go silent so quickly.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Hardly had the audience begun to whisper when Mateo switched on his phone torch.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: And not only did he do that, but he also got the whole front row to do the same.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Beautiful. And when did the electricity come back?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Not until the last song did the lights return — so the choir sang the entire concert by torchlight.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Little did we know that the video would get thirty thousand views by Sunday.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Rarely does a power cut turn into good publicity. One last sentence, Liam — a rule for next time?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Under no circumstances should anyone plug a fog machine into the same socket as the stage lights.

items.why: inversion in the main clause with did

items.second_end: the emergency exit unless there is a fire.

summary: Front a negative or limiting adverbial and invert auxiliary and subject: Never have I…
No auxiliary? Add do / does / did and keep the bare infinitive: Rarely does she complain.
No sooner … than; hardly / scarcely … when; not until / only when + clause, then invert the main clause.
Not only inverts the first clause only; so / such … that inverts with be.
Use it for emphasis and formality — a couple of times in an essay, not in every sentence.
